name: Fear of missing out
statement: People who fear that others are having rewarding experiences without them report using social media more, and report worse mood and lower life satisfaction.
meaning: Przybylski and colleagues define fear of missing out as a pervasive apprehension that others might be having rewarding experiences from which one is absent, marked by a desire to stay continually connected with what others are doing. It is framed as an individual difference, a trait some people carry more of, rather than a state a situation produces. Everything in the founding paper rests on one self-report instrument, the ten-item Fear of Missing Out scale. Two of its ten items are about behaviour rather than fear: item 8 asks whether sharing details of a good time online is important, item 10 whether the respondent keeps tabs on friends while on holiday. That matters because the finding the construct is famous for is a correlation between this scale and self-reported social media use, and part of the scale is already asking about social media use.

origin.who: Andrew K. Przybylski, Kou Murayama, Cody R. DeHaan and Valerie Gladwell
origin.note: Three cross-sectional studies that built the scale and mapped its correlates. The term was already in circulation: the paper cites two 2011 and 2012 trend reports by the marketing agency JWT and columns in the New York Times and San Francisco Chronicle as the writing it drafted its items from.

evidence: Study 1 gave 32 candidate items to 1,013 Mechanical Turk workers, 672 men and 341 women, aged 18 to 62, of whom 41.1% lived in the United States and 35.9% in India. Confirmatory factor analysis cut the pool to 25 items, and item response theory picked the final ten, which showed maximum information at a latent trait level of 0.51 and an alpha of .87. Study 2 ran the scale on a Harris Poll panel of 2,079 working-age adults in Great Britain, 1,040 men and 1,039 women aged 22 to 65, in late September 2011. FoMO correlated -.37 with age, -.29 with psychological need satisfaction, -.24 with general mood, -.19 with life satisfaction and .40 with social media engagement, which was measured by five questions about using social media around waking, meals and sleep. Mediation analysis found that need satisfaction, mood and life satisfaction predicted social media engagement only through FoMO, with the direct paths falling to non-significance. Study 3 tested 87 first-year students, 20 men and 67 women. FoMO predicted Facebook engagement at b = .41, negative affect while using Facebook at .40, positive affect at .31, Facebook use during lectures at .27 and self-reported distracted driving at .28. All three studies were one-time surveys, and the authors say so, writing that future work in experimental settings would allow causal models to be evaluated.

replication.headline: The correlation with social media use reproduces at scale and comes out close to the original, .41 against .40, while the scale's single-factor structure and the causal story attached to it do not hold up.
replication.detail: Akbari and colleagues pooled 86 effect sizes covering 55,134 participants, mean age 22.07, 58.37% female. Trait FoMO correlated with internet use at r = 0.41, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.44. That is a close match to the .40 Przybylski reported in a single British panel. It is also heterogeneous to the point where the average is a poor summary: I-squared was 94.04, and the 95% prediction interval runs from 0.11 to 0.63, so a future sample could show almost nothing. Facebook use gave r = 0.35, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.42, from 11 samples; Instagram use gave r = 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.64, from three. The only moderator that reached significance was the pandemic, with 58 pre-COVID samples at r = 0.38 and 14 later ones at r = 0.54. Zhang, Li and Yu's meta-analysis of 65 studies and 70 effect sizes reports r = 0.38, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.41, and finds the number varies by what is measured: addiction 0.47, intensity 0.32, duration 0.25, frequency 0.14. Frequency of use, the most literal reading of 'uses social media more', is the weakest link in that set. The structure of the scale is where replication fails outright. Groenestein and colleagues tested it on 2,041 Dutch social media users and found a second-order construct with two dimensions, pervasive apprehension and desire for connection, fitting better than one factor. The dimensions behave differently: apprehension tracks problematic social media use, need deficits and neuroticism, while desire for connection tracks ordinary use frequency and extraversion. Elhai, Gazit, Casale and Montag replicated the split in 388 American students and found that desire for connection was the more strongly associated with problematic smartphone use, and that the two dimensions related equally to depression, anxiety, rumination and distress tolerance. On direction, Li and colleagues followed 1,419 Dutch adolescents aged 11 to 15 across four annual waves from 2015 to 2019 with a random intercept cross-lagged panel model. Within persons, FoMO raised problematic social media use in mid-adolescence and problematic use did not raise FoMO, and low life satisfaction predicted later FoMO in early adolescents. That is one study, in one country, on problematic use rather than use.

study.cite: Akbari, M., Seydavi, M., Palmieri, S., Mansueto, G., Caselli, G., & Spada, M. M. (2021). Fear of missing out (FoMO) and internet use: A comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Behavioral Addictions, 10(4), 879-900.

limits: Almost the whole literature is cross-sectional self-report, and the two things being correlated are measured minutes apart in the same questionnaire. Akbari and colleagues state the limit plainly: findings should be read in light of the observational nature of the review, and causality could not be inferred given the cross-sectional design of the included studies. Their samples were also 45% Asian, 32% European and 19% American, and young, so the pooled figure is not a general population figure. Several numbers could not be obtained for this entry. Fioravanti and colleagues' 2021 meta-analysis in Computers in Human Behavior is named here as existing; ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 and no effect size from it appears above. Zhang, Li and Yu's figures are read from the journal's own English abstract page, and their total participant count is not stated there. Li and colleagues' cross-lagged coefficients are described from the abstract at the Vrije Universiteit repository, not from the article, so no numbers from it are printed. Milyavskaya and colleagues' experience-sampling study of college freshmen reports that FoMO occurred often, more later in the day and week and during required tasks, and tracked negative affect, fatigue, stress, physical symptoms and lost sleep; its sample sizes and effect sizes were not in the abstract obtained and are not quoted. Searches covered Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, PMC, Springer, ScienceDirect, Cyberpsychology, Acta Psychologica Sinica and general web search.
misreadings: The prevalence claim is the loudest error. The figure that nearly three quarters of young adults experience FoMO comes from JWT trend reports of 2011 and 2012, which is where this entry reads it, in Przybylski's summary of them. It is marketing research, not a measured prevalence, and the founding paper describes it as preliminary industry work. The second error is causal. A correlation of about .4 between two questionnaires filled in at the same sitting does not show that social media produces FoMO, or that FoMO drives people to social media, and the one four-wave study located here points the arrow from FoMO to problematic use rather than back. The third is treating FoMO research as part of the screen-time debate. Orben and Przybylski's specification curve analysis of three datasets, 355,358 adolescents, found digital technology use explained at most 0.4% of the variation in well-being, with a median standardised coefficient of -0.035 in one dataset and associations comparable to eating potatoes or wearing glasses. That is a different measure of a different thing, and it is not a small-effect verdict on FoMO. The last is that FoMO is one quantity. Two large samples now say the scale carries two dimensions that correlate with different things, so a short form that drops items from one of them measures something other than what the original scale measured.
